title: Heuristic-driven prefix signature and eviction policy for cross-request KV reuse
creator: Maya Chen
description: Improve cross-request prefix reuse by introducing compact runtime signatures and an eviction policy that prioritizes long-lived coherent prefixes while bounding GPU memory. Goal: increase prompt-cache hit rate in continuous-batching workloads without increasing worst-case memory usage or adding high CPU overhead.
background: We currently store KV cache fragments per request and perform some dedupe based on exact-match keys. In high-concurrency continuous-batching scenarios (many short prompts with shared prefixes), we observe suboptimal reuse because: 1) small edits to prompts break equality, 2) storing many near-duplicate fragments inflates GPU memory, 3) eviction is primarily time-based, which can evict fragments still valuable across concurrent requests.
problem_statement: Design and implement a low-cost, collision-safe signature for prefix fragments and an eviction policy that prefers keeping fragments likely to be reused across the current batch window and near-future requests, while providing strict upper bounds on GPU resident memory.
proposed_solution: 1) Compact fragment signature: compute a 64-bit signature per prefix fragment combining a stable hash (SipHash keyed with runtime secret) and a small locality-sensitive component (n-gram fingerprint). Store signatures in a compact index in CPU memory; only resident fragments keep full KV tensors on GPU. 2) Heuristic reuse score: maintain per-signature counters (global and sliding-window) and a coalescing counter for the number of concurrent batches referencing the signature. 3) Eviction policy: multi-factor score = alpha*reuse_score + beta*recency - gamma*memory_cost. On memory pressure, evict lowest score fragments first. 4) Continuous-batching hooks: when forming batches, consult signatures of queued requests to pin high-coalescing fragments to GPU for the duration of the batch, avoiding repeated transfer. 5) Safe dedupe: when two fragments have identical signatures we verify by lightweight token-prefix length check to avoid rare collisions before performing full dedupe/merge. 6) Adaptive chunking: split large KV fragments into fixed-size shards to avoid large allocation spikes and make eviction/transfer more granular.
design_decisions: - Use 64-bit signatures: balances collision rate vs index size. - Register a runtime secret for SipHash per process to prevent cross-tenant inference of signatures. - Keep signature metadata on CPU to reduce GPU residency. - Shard size default 256KB (empirically tuned) but configurable per-model. - Eviction policy parameters alpha/beta/gamma exposed via runtime config and feature flags to enable safe ramp.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): implement signature + CPU index and read-only cache lookup, no eviction changes (runtime flag off by default). Deploy to dedicated small canary fleet for 2 weeks using synthetic prefix-heavy workloads. Phase 2 (gradual): enable heuristic reuse scoring and pinning for batches on 10% of traffic; monitor memory and latency. Phase 3 (ramp): enable eviction policy with conservative gamma to start; expand to 50% and then 100% once stability metrics are met.
performance_targets: - Increase prefix-level cache hit rate by at least 20% on internal prefix-heavy benchmarks. - No increase in 95th percentile generation latency > 5ms. - Reduce GPU memory churn (bytes transferred per minute) by 30% in continuous-batching tests. - Eviction/reactivation should not exceed 2% additional CPU utilization on median nodes.
testing_plan: - Unit tests for signature computation, collision verification, and shard boundary correctness. - Synthetic load tests: short shared-prefix workload, adversarial near-duplicate workload, and long-sequence workload to validate shard reassembly. - Chaos test: force repeated evictions and verify no correctness regressions. - A/B on canary with telemetry: prefix hit rate, memory resident bytes, transfer counts, tail latency, and CPU usage.
acceptance_criteria: 1) All unit and integration tests pass. 2) Canary metrics meet performance targets for 2 consecutive weeks. 3) No observed correctness errors (generation divergence) in canary. 4) Rollout playbook (rollback steps + feature flags) documented and reviewed.
tasks: Implement SipHash-based 64-bit signature util (C++ runtime + Python SDK shim)
Design CPU-resident compact index and APIs for lookup/insert/remove
Implement shard layout for KV fragments and GPU transfer abstractions
Implement reuse counters and sliding-window coalescing counter
Add heuristic scoring and eviction loop respecting GPU memory budget
Add batch pinning logic in the scheduler to hold high-score shards during batch lifetime
Instrumentation: telemetry for hit/miss, collisions, evictions, memory transfers
End-to-end integration tests and synthetic workload harness
Canary deployment and monitoring dashboard setup
Documentation: runtime flags, config knobs, and operator runbook
risks_and_mitigation: Collision risk: mitigated by a cheap verification step (token-length + partial hash) before dedupe
Memory fragmentation: mitigated via fixed-size sharding and periodic compaction during low-load windows
CPU overhead from metadata updates: keep counters approximate (atomic increment with periodic aggregation) and sample under heavy load
Regression in latency: conservative rollout and ability to disable pinning/eviction via flags
notes: This approach intentionally avoids full content fingerprinting which is expensive and leaks possible prompt semantics. The signature + light verify step provides a practical tradeoff.
We should evaluate alternative LSH techniques if 64-bit proves too collision-prone for some customer workloads.
Coordination required with Scheduling and Dedicated teams to ensure pinning doesn't cause noisy neighbor effects on multi-tenant nodes.

implementation_notes: Keep signature computation outside critical token-generation path; compute on request enqueue. Make metadata updates lock-free where possible and bounded to amortize CPU cost. Provide a telemetry-enabled fallback that disables signature-based dedupe if collision rate > threshold.
retrospective_success_metrics: Post-rollout the ticket can be closed when: 1) at least one production customer shows >15% cost reduction on inference-heavy endpoints due to reduced token compute, or 2) internal benchmarks show target hit-rate and memory improvements for 4 weeks.
